source.title: TMallGS: Scaling Unified Feature and Sequence Modeling for Generative E-commerce Search
source.authors: Zhen-Tao Song; Yufeng Gao; Xing-Ye Fang; Jing Wang; Guang-Xin Song; Bo-Kang Wang; Yi-Pin Dai; Heng-Liang Guo

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether increased scale improves performance using a different measure and setting: ranking performance for an industrial recommendation model, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study’s scaling sweep reports a monotonic performance trend across width, depth, and sequence length. The scaling plot’s numerical values are not available in the supplied text. Other model comparisons, component ablations, warm-up results, and online business metrics are not rows because they do not report outcomes of the scaling sweep.
record.test_reason: The study uses LLM scaling laws as motivation and reports that its own CTR ranking model gains AUC/GAUC monotonically with compute across width, depth and sequence-length sweeps. It fits no power law and reports no held-out loss, exponents, extrapolation or allocation. The system is a task-trained recommender, not a pretrained language model. The only result is a qualitative 'monotonic gains' statement about Figure 2, which cannot show any version's power-law form or downstream predictability. The record's T2 'tests V6' overreaches: V6 concerns downstream performance of pretrained language models predicted from scale or pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude TmallGS breaks the DLRM performance ceiling and adheres to neural scaling laws with predictable gains from more compute. This rests only on qualitative monotonic trends in Figure 2, with no fitted law. Billion-parameter scaling is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Measures ranking performance in an industrial recommendation system while varying width, depth, and sequence length; it does not fit language-model cross-entropy power laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling dimension changes the reported trend: depth has the steepest trajectory, while length is described as growing linearly through T = 1500.

fits_no_version.finding: A CTR ranking Transformer (TmallGS) shows monotonic AUC/GAUC gains over a cold-start DIN baseline as GFLOPs grow via width (512–1024), depth (4–10) or sequence length (500–1500). Depth has the steepest trajectory, and length shows no saturation up to 1500.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task performance of Transformer recommendation/ranking models improves monotonically with compute along width, depth and sequence length (qualitative, no fitted law).

record.peer_reviewed: KDD ’26, Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
record.problems: The scaling section gives qualitative trends but no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. It reports no fitted scaling exponents, extrapolation test, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-sweep conditions were omitted. Numerical values shown only in Figure 2 could not be extracted from the supplied text.

untested.parts: All: width and depth are varied with compute, not at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other domains: the recommender sweep gives no fitted form or loss values.
All: no downstream evaluation of pretrained language models.
All: no fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Numerical values, metric (AUC vs GAUC) and axis scale of the Figure 2 scaling curves; needed to judge any functional form.
missing.versions: none (would bear on V5 if a loss or fitted form were shown)

missing.what: Deployment choice prioritises sequence length over depth, 'guided by the Scaling Law analysis', even though depth was reported as the steepest. The choice was driven by latency constraints, not a compute-optimal fit.

record.verdict_notes: Industrial CTR ranking paper (KDD '26). The scaling claim is asserted rather than fitted: three points per dimension, no loss, no exponents, no uncertainty. The record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' is wrong for the scaling sweep; only the online A/B test reports p<0.05. The deployed dense backbone is about 0.05B parameters.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how either quantity grows with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests ranking performance against model scaling, but not performance predicted from pretraining loss or across downstream tasks.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and systematic departures from a single power law.
